prompt: A struct and a class each have two stored properties with no default value and no `init` written. Which one compiles?
hint: What does the compiler write for one of them?

choices.text: The struct
choices.why: Right: it gets a memberwise initialiser; the class gets `has no initializers`.

choices.text: The class
choices.why: The class is the one refused, with a note under each property.

choices.text: Both, with default values of zero and the empty string
choices.why: Swift invents no default value for a property.

choices.text: Neither, until both have an `init`
choices.why: The struct compiled without one.

prompt: `print(second)` for an instance of `final class SessionRef`, compiled with `swiftc KindsFixed.swift -o kindsfixed`, printed `kindsfixed.SessionRef`. Why not its properties?

choices.text: Because `final` hides the properties from `print`
choices.why: `final` only forbids subclasses.

choices.text: Because the properties are `var`
choices.why: The struct's are `var` too, and it printed them.

choices.text: A class is described by its identity, not by its contents
choices.why: Right: a struct is described by its contents, a class instance by its identity.

choices.text: Because the program was compiled, not run with `swift`
choices.why: Both commands print a class the same way.

prompt: Which of these does a `class` have and a `struct` does not? Choose all that apply.
hint: The table at the end of section 02.

choices.text: Inheritance from a superclass
choices.why: Yes, unless the class is `final`.
Yes: identity only exists for references.

choices.text: Stored properties
choices.why: Both have them.

choices.text: `deinit`
choices.why: Yes: code that runs when the instance goes away, lesson 11.

choices.text: Methods
choices.why: Both have them; a struct's that change it are `mutating`.

prompt: `var monday = StudySession(course: "Swift", minutes: 45)`, a struct. Then `var tuesday = monday` and `tuesday.minutes = 60`. What is `monday.minutes`?
Why does `func extend(_ session: StudySession) { session.minutes += 15 }` not compile?
hint: What kind of name is a parameter?

choices.text: `+=` does not work on properties
choices.why: It does, on a `var`; `Copies.swift` used it on `longer.minutes`.

choices.text: A parameter is a `let`, a constant copy
choices.why: Right: `'session' is a 'let' constant`. Copy it into a `var` and return the new value.

choices.text: The function has no return type
choices.why: A function may return nothing; the error is about the parameter.

choices.text: Structs cannot be passed to functions without `inout`
choices.why: They can, and they arrive as copies.

prompt: `var week = [monday, tuesday]` holds two `StudySession` structs. `var copy = week; copy[0].minutes = 0`. Which line is true afterwards?
hint: An array of values is a value.

choices.text: `week[0].minutes` is 0 too, because arrays are shared
choices.why: Arrays share a buffer only until somebody writes, and this was a write.

choices.text: `monday.minutes` is 0, as the array held it
choices.why: The array held a copy of `monday` from the moment it was built.

choices.text: It does not compile: an element of an array is a constant
choices.why: `copy` is a `var`, so its elements can change.

choices.text: Only `copy[0].minutes` is 0
choices.why: Right: the program printed `45 0`.

prompt: Same as before, but `StudySession` is a `final class`: `let monday = StudySession(course: "Swift", minutes: 45)`, `let tuesday = monday`, `tuesday.minutes = 60`. What is `monday.minutes`?
`let monday` holds a class instance, and `monday.minutes = 0` compiles. Why is the `let` not refusing it?

choices.text: Class properties ignore `let` and `var` altogether
choices.why: A `let` property of a class still cannot change.

choices.text: The `let` fixes the reference, and the instance's `var` properties stay changeable
choices.why: Right: `monday` will always reach the same session; that session's minutes are free.

choices.text: It is a compiler bug in Swift 6.4.2
choices.why: It is the defined meaning of `let` for a reference.

choices.text: `minutes` is `mutating`
choices.why: `mutating` is a word for struct methods.

prompt: A function takes a `StudySession` class instance and sets its minutes to 0. The caller's code has no `&` and no `inout`. What does the caller's session show afterwards?

choices.text: Its old minutes, as the function had a copy
choices.why: That is the struct case; a class parameter is a copy of the reference.

choices.text: A compile error, as the parameter is a `let`
choices.why: The `let` fixes the reference, and the property may still change.
Right: one instance, reached by both, and nothing at the call site warned the reader.

choices.text: A crash, for a shared instance changed without permission
choices.why: Nothing checks that; this is ordinary class behaviour.

prompt: A struct method appends to one of the struct's arrays. What does it need in front of `func`?

choices.text: `inout`
choices.why: `inout` marks a parameter, not a method.

choices.text: `mutating`
choices.why: Right: the note said `mark method 'mutating' to make 'self' mutable`.

choices.text: `var`
choices.why: `var` names a variable; a method is not one.

choices.text: `final`, so nobody overrides the change
choices.why: `final` is for classes, and structs have no subclasses.

prompt: `let frozen = Week(minutes: [45, 30])`, and `Week` has `mutating func add` and a plain `func total`. Which call compiles?
hint: A `let` struct cannot change at all.

choices.text: `frozen.add(60)`
choices.why: Refused: `cannot use mutating member on immutable value`.

choices.text: `frozen.total()`
choices.why: Right: it reads and changes nothing, so a `let` is enough.

choices.text: Both, because `frozen` was initialised with values
choices.why: How it was built does not matter; it is a `let`.

choices.text: Neither of them, until `frozen` is changed into a `var` declaration
choices.why: Non-mutating methods work on a `let`.

prompt: Inside an ordinary struct method, the value the method was called on, `___`, is a constant.
`x` and `y` are two instances of a class, each with 45 minutes, and `z = x`. What does `print(x === y, x === z)` print?

choices.text: `true true`
choices.why: `x` and `y` are two instances, whatever they hold.

choices.text: `false true`
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: `true false`
choices.why: `z` is a second name for `x`'s instance.

choices.text: It does not compile without `Equatable`
choices.why: `===` needs nothing; `==` is the one that does.

prompt: What made `a == b` compile for `struct SessionValue`?

choices.text: Structs compare with `==` always, with nothing declared
choices.why: Without a declared conformance there is no `==`.

choices.text: A `==` function written below the struct
choices.why: None was written.

choices.text: `: Equatable`, and the compiler wrote the comparison
choices.why: Right: every stored property is equatable, so the compiler compares them all.

choices.text: Both values were created with the same literal
choices.why: How a value was made does not give it an operator.

prompt: Why does the compiler refuse to write `==` for a class, when it writes it for a struct?
hint: Two accounts with the same name.

choices.text: For a class, equality is a decision about meaning
choices.why: Right: two instances with equal contents may still be two different things in the world.

choices.text: Classes cannot conform to `Equatable` under any circumstances
choices.why: They can; you write the `==`, as lesson 8 shows.

choices.text: Comparing properties of a class is slower than of a struct
choices.why: Speed is not the reason; meaning is.

choices.text: `===` already does the same job
choices.why: `===` asks a different question: the same instance, not equal contents.

prompt: `var copy = week`, then `copy.append(90)`. When were `week`'s elements actually copied?
hint: Section 07 asked each array where its buffer was.

choices.text: At `var copy = week`
choices.why: The buffers were still the same after the assignment.

choices.text: At the `append`
choices.why: Right: the first write to a shared buffer is the moment it is copied.

choices.text: Never, as both share one buffer for good
choices.why: Then `week` would have four elements; it kept three.

choices.text: When `print` read them
choices.why: Reading never copies.

prompt: A struct `Log` holds a class `Storage`, with no `isKnownUniquelyReferenced` check. `var tuesday = monday; tuesday.add(30)`. What happens to `monday`?

choices.text: Nothing: a struct is copied, so its storage is copied with it
choices.why: The struct is copied, and so is the reference inside it, not the instance.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a class inside a struct
choices.why: It accepts it; that is why the check exists.

choices.text: It gains the 30 as well, through the shared storage
choices.why: Right: both logs reach one `Storage`, so the struct behaves like a class.

choices.text: `monday` crashes the next time it is read
choices.why: Nothing crashes; the change is silent, which is the danger.

prompt: Arrays copy their elements only when one of the sharers writes. The technique is called copy-on-___.
Which of these does Apple's "Choosing Between Structures and Classes" give as a reason for a class?

choices.text: A type with more than ten properties
choices.why: Size is not one of the reasons; copy-on-write makes large values cheap.

choices.text: Identity matters: every part must see one instance
choices.why: Right, with Objective-C interoperability and inheritance as the other two.

choices.text: Any type that has methods
choices.why: Structs have methods.

choices.text: A type that will be compared with `==`
choices.why: Structs get `==` from the compiler more readily than classes.

prompt: In `Choosing.swift`, `var edited = store.sessions[0]; edited.minutes = 90`. Why did the week screen still print `[45, 30]`?
hint: What type is a session there?

choices.text: The screen caches what it printed the first time
choices.why: `show` reads the store every time.

choices.text: `PlannerStore` is a struct, so the screens had copies of it
choices.why: It is a class; both screens saw both added sessions.

choices.text: `StudySession` is a struct, so `edited` was a copy
choices.why: Right: writing it back into `store.sessions[0]` is the visible step that would change the store.

choices.text: `edited.minutes = 90` is ignored outside a `mutating` method
choices.why: It changed `edited`; `edited` is not in the store.

pairs.left: `var a = S(minutes: 45); var b = a; b.minutes = 60; print(a.minutes)`
`let a = C(minutes: 45); let b = a; b.minutes = 60; print(a.minutes)`

items: `monday.add(45)` finds its storage unshared and writes in place
`tuesday = monday` copies the struct and the reference inside it
`tuesday.add(30)` finds the storage shared and copies it

prompt: A planner needs a list of sessions that two screens both read and change, each seeing the other's changes. What should hold the list?
hint: Section 08's shape: values for data, one reference for the place.

choices.text: A struct that each screen keeps its own copy of
choices.why: Then each screen sees only its own changes.

choices.text: A global `let` array that both screens read
choices.why: A `let` array cannot be changed.

choices.text: Each screen's own array, kept in step by hand
choices.why: Two copies kept equal by hand is the bug a shared instance avoids.

choices.text: One class instance both screens reference
choices.why: Right: `PlannerStore`, holding `StudySession` values.
